A. Measuring roof runoff began as Project 101 at a technical college. The team wanted to measure delayed runoff. The investigation started in summer and lasted 8 weeks. Staff had previously relied on occasional observations, which could miss short changes. They therefore installed a small demonstration unit beside the existing system. The trial was intended to compare local measurements, not to establish a rule for every building.

B. The demonstration unit processed rainwater. Material entered through an inlet at the left and first crossed a removable screen. It then passed through fine mesh held in the central treatment bed. Immediately after this bed, a level sensor recorded the condition of the moving material. The material finally entered a measuring tank on the right. A small sampling port was fitted below the instrument.

C. The experimental units received the new treatment bed. The control units used the previous arrangement. Both groups were inspected at the same time each morning. The experimental group showed lower variation in its readings during the trial. However, its inspection costs were higher. The team did not record whether the units reduced total energy use.

D. Dr Patel argued that installation should wait until long-term records were available. Dr Evans preferred a limited trial in additional buildings before any wider decision. Dr Silva considered the system useful only where trained staff could check it regularly. Their disagreement concerned the evidence needed for expansion, rather than whether the trial had taken place. The site manager had suggested testing a different arrangement around the roof tiles, but that idea was not evaluated in this study. No researcher claimed that one design would be suitable everywhere.

Conditions outside the unit, including wind-driven rain, could also influence readings. The writer rejects the idea that a short successful trial makes further monitoring unnecessary. A sensible next step is independent replication, using sites with different operating conditions.

Establishing that distinction required an explicit comparison rather than an isolated favourable reading.

B. The demonstration unit processed wastewater. Material entered through an inlet at the left and first crossed a removable screen. It then passed through ceramic beads held in the central treatment bed. Immediately after this bed, a turbidity sensor recorded the condition of the moving material. A reading taken before the bed would have described incoming conditions, whereas the instrument in this arrangement described material after treatment. Confusing those positions would therefore change the interpretation of the same numerical value. Location was part of the method, not a decorative feature of the diagram.

sections.title: Reading Passage
sections.passage:
A. Conserving timber specimens began as Project 119 at a conservation laboratory. The team wanted to keep experimental conditions stable. The investigation started in winter and lasted 14 weeks. Staff had previously relied on occasional observations, which could miss short changes. They therefore installed a small demonstration unit beside the existing system. The trial was intended to compare local measurements, not to establish a rule for every building. Participants recorded operating conditions in a shared log, so that an unusual reading could be checked against what had happened that day. The question, although prompted by an operational inconvenience, was therefore methodological as well as practical: could a routinely collected signal sustain a defensible comparison? The team restricted its claim to the observed setting precisely because the convenience of collecting a number does not establish either its relevance to a broader outcome or its stability elsewhere.

B. The demonstration unit processed air. Material entered through an inlet at the left and first crossed a removable screen. It then passed through zeolite pellets held in the central treatment bed. Immediately after this bed, a temperature sensor recorded the condition of the moving material. The material finally entered a conditioning chamber on the right. A small sampling port was fitted below the instrument. Staff took a reference sample there before emptying the vessel. The screen could be removed without disturbing the bed. A cover protected the apparatus, but it was not part of the treatment route. The physical sequence also established the boundaries of interpretation. An observation made at the designated position could describe material leaving the bed, but could not by itself reconstruct all the changes that had occurred upstream. Checking the reference sample reduced reliance on a single instrument without converting two imperfect observations into a complete account of the process.

C. The comparison used two groups of units. The experimental units received the new treatment bed, whereas the control units used the previous arrangement. Both groups were inspected at the same time each morning. The experimental group showed lower variation in its readings during the trial. However, its calibration costs were higher. The team did not record whether the units reduced total energy use. Some early readings were excluded because the instruments had not yet been calibrated. The report identified these exclusions rather than treating the missing measurements as evidence of improvement. In principle, a treatment might make a measured outcome more consistent while imposing costs that undermine its practical value. That possibility does not refute the observed reduction in variation; it limits the conclusion that may reasonably be drawn from it. Likewise, a quantity that was not measured cannot legitimately be inferred merely because another quantity moved in a desirable direction.

D. Dr Ali argued that installation should wait until long-term records were available. Dr Nolan preferred a limited trial in additional buildings before any wider decision. Dr Reed considered the system useful only where trained staff could check it regularly. Their disagreement concerned the evidence needed for expansion, rather than whether the trial had taken place. The site manager had suggested testing a different arrangement around the specimen racks, but that idea was not evaluated in this study. No researcher claimed that one design would be suitable everywhere. Read superficially, these recommendations might appear to express the same general caution. Their implications are nevertheless different: a demand for duration, a demand for a wider but restricted comparison and a demand for operational competence specify distinct conditions of acceptance. A recommendation conditional on one of them cannot be attributed to a researcher who proposed another.

E. The writer considers the local result promising but insufficient for universal adoption. Lower variation alone does not establish that the treatment bed caused every observed change. Conditions outside the unit, including changes in room temperature, could also influence readings. The writer rejects the idea that a short successful trial makes further monitoring unnecessary. A sensible next step is independent replication, using sites with different operating conditions. A decision about expansion should compare benefits with the extra calibration burden and should distinguish measured outcomes from attractive but untested explanations. The strongest version of the competing argument is that decisions must sometimes precede complete knowledge. The writer accepts that practical constraint but denies that it erases the distinction between a reversible local experiment and general adoption. What remains necessary is a transparent account of the uncertainties being accepted, rather than confidence manufactured by restating a limited finding in universal language.
